overview: A servo motor is a small motor with a built-in gearbox and feedback circuit that lets you command it to hold a specific angle, rather than just spinning continuously like a normal DC motor. The SG90 is the classic entry-level hobby servo: light, cheap, plastic-geared, and strong enough for small mechanisms like a robotic arm joint or a pan-tilt camera mount. You tell it where to point using a PWM signal, and it uses its internal electronics to drive itself to that angle and hold position against a moderate load. It belongs to the family of RC hobby servos, the same category used in remote-control cars and planes.

specifications.rotationRange: ~180 degrees (standard variant); continuous-rotation variants exist and behave differently
specifications.pulseWidthRange: ~1ms (0 degrees) to ~2ms (180 degrees), 1.5ms neutral/center — exact range varies slightly by unit

pinMap.name: Signal (orange/yellow wire)
pinMap.function: Receives the PWM control pulse that tells the servo what angle to move to. The pulse repeats roughly every 20ms (50Hz); the width of the HIGH portion (1-2ms) encodes the target angle.
pinMap.gotcha: Needs a clean, regularly repeating pulse — software-based 'bit-banged' timing on a busy microcontroller can cause visible jitter. Dedicated libraries (e.g., the Arduino Servo library) or hardware PWM avoid this.

pinMap.name: VCC (red wire)
pinMap.function: Power input driving the internal motor and gearbox.
pinMap.currentLimit: Can spike to 500mA-700mA+ under load or stall, far more than a microcontroller's onboard 5V pin can safely supply for more than one servo
pinMap.gotcha: Powering more than one or two servos directly from a microcontroller board's 5V pin is a very common failure mode — it browns out the board, causing random resets or erratic behavior. Use a separate 5V supply for multiple or high-load servos.

pinMap.name: GND (brown/black wire)
pinMap.function: Ground return for the motor power circuit.
pinMap.gotcha: If the servo is powered from a separate supply (recommended for multiple servos), that supply's ground must still be tied to the microcontroller's ground, or the signal reference will float and the servo will behave erratically.

useCases.title: Robotic arm joint
useCases.scenario: Use one servo per joint (base rotation, shoulder, elbow, gripper) to build a simple 3-4 degree-of-freedom arm.

useCases.title: Pan-tilt camera/sensor mount
useCases.scenario: Two servos mounted perpendicular to each other let a camera or an HC-SR04 sensor sweep across a wider field of view.

useCases.title: RC car steering
useCases.scenario: A single servo turns the front wheels left/right based on a receiver or microcontroller signal.

useCases.title: Sorting mechanism gate
useCases.scenario: Servo rotates a small flap or gate to direct items into different bins based on a sensor reading (e.g., color or size detection upstream).

useCases.title: Automatic pet feeder flap
useCases.scenario: Servo opens a food-dispensing flap on a timer or button press, then returns to the closed angle.

oftenConfusedWith: Continuous-rotation servos (same form factor, but the signal controls speed/direction instead of a fixed angle)
Stepper motors (higher precision and holding torque, but need a dedicated driver and more complex control)
oftenUpgradedTo: MG90S / MG996R (metal-geared servos with higher torque and durability)

beginnerMistakes: Powering multiple servos straight from the microcontroller's 5V pin, causing brownouts and random resets.
Forcing the horn to rotate by hand while powered off — this can strip the internal plastic gears.
Commanding an angle outside the servo's actual mechanical range, causing it to stall, buzz, and draw excess current against its own end-stop.
Forgetting a common ground when using a separate power supply, causing jittery or random movement.
